brief: A single pair of grey felt valenki boots standing in a snowdrift, rendered with obsessive realism yet carrying the warmth of a Soviet children's-book page. Flat gouache-like watercolour fields of brick red, mustard ochre and cold turquoise sky sit behind the boots like a printed backdrop. The boots themselves are built up in dense, patient coloured pencil: every matted wool fibre, every crust of snow clinging to the soles, a pale crack where the felt has creased. Edges of the background stay crisp and slightly off-register. Low winter light from the left, cheerful, never sentimental.

An old man's forearm resting on a tabletop, his skin loose and freckled, carrying a decades-old sailor tattoo of a swallow and anchor blurred to faded indigo. The palette is drawn from washed denim: grey-blue, chalky indigo, bleached white, and a single tan of sun-worn skin. Fine crosshatching follows the arm's contour like twill weave, and watercolour bleeds give the ink its soft migration under the skin. Raised veins, silver hairs and wrinkles are rendered with hyperreal care. Quiet, tender, documentary.

Two fresh mackerel lying head to tail on a wooden board, their tiger-striped backs rendered in exacting hyperreal detail. The handling borrows katazome's stencil dyeing: flat resist shapes, softened rinsed edges, and a textured cloth-like ground in persimmon rust and soot black. The iridescent silver-green bellies and wet eyes are built in glazed watercolour with crisp pen highlights. A repeating stencilled wave pattern, slightly irregular, fills the background. Deliberate, crafted, cool, the fish gleaming against the dyed ground.

A child's bicycle wheel half-sunk in a roadside runnel of spring meltwater, grey slush banks crumbling on either side. The water is clear and moving, painted with hyperreal refraction: bent spokes beneath the surface, grit on the tarmac below, a tiny rushing standing wave. Watercolour in muddy olive, cold steel blue and slate is laid wet-on-wet for the slush, with crisp pen lines for chrome, reflections and pitted rust. Low raking March sunlight glints off the wet surfaces. Fresh, cold, transitional.

A pink and yellow concha sweet bun on a market table, its cracked sugar crust and soft crumb rendered in hyperreal detail. Above, unseen, hang punched tissue-paper banners: their light filters onto the scene as dappled patches of magenta, lime, tangerine and turquoise. Translucent watercolour glazes overlap where colours mix, and hard-edged patches of light fall across the oilcloth, bun and a chipped clay mug. Fine coloured pencil captures the sugar granules and the oilcloth's gingham weave. Festive, warm, sunlit noon.

The end of a weathered pine fruit crate filling the frame, its peeling paper label printed in flat, saturated lithographic colour: a stylised sunburst in cadmium orange and cobalt. Resting against the crate, a real blood orange cut in half, painted with startling hyperreal juiciness: glistening crimson-and-amber segments, pith fibres, a drop of juice running down. Spray-soft gradients give the label its period airbrush glow, and dry-brushed pencil grain shows the wood under torn paper. The contrast is the point: commercial idealisation beside the actual fruit, both equally vivid.

A strand of rusted barbed wire on a fence post, coated in rime ice that has grown in feathery, wind-aligned crystals along one side only. The near-monochrome palette is white, pearl grey and pale blue-violet, with tiny flecks of rust orange where the wire shows through. Feather-fine pen strokes build each crystal spine; sharp white edges are kept from the toned grey paper. The background is fog, rendered as flat soft charcoal haze. Cold, brittle, silent, with directional rhythm everywhere.

A red cabbage sliced cleanly in half, shown head-on and nearly mirror-symmetrical, echoing the stacked layers of a Polish paper-cut. Its convoluted white veins and deep magenta-violet folds read as cut layers, yet every surface is hyperreal: moisture beads on the cut face, bloom on the outer leaves, a knife-scored edge. Behind it, a flat field of saturated emerald with a crisp scalloped border in cut-paper black. Watercolour glazes build the violet's depth; fine pen traces each vein. Folk symmetry and kitchen reality fused.

A single wooden match caught at the instant of ignition, set on a steep diagonal across an off-white ground like a Bauhaus poster. A flat vermilion disc sits behind the flame, a black bar cuts the lower third, and a thin yellow rule anchors the corner. Inside this graphic order the match is completely real: splintered pine grain, the bubbling sulphur head, a curl of grey smoke and the translucent blue base of the flame. Hard-edged marker fills for the geometry and fine graphite and watercolour for the object. Tense, economical, mechanical.

A hyperreal overhead view of a tortoise's domed shell, every scute rendered with true volume and growth ridges. The surface texture is built entirely in the Gond manner, from dense rhythmic fills of tiny dashes, dots and hairline strokes in vermilion, turmeric yellow, leaf green and white over a warm umber ground. The pattern follows each plate's contours like fingerprint ridges, so form and ornament become one. The scaly head and claws peek out at the edges. Lively and devotional.

A string of drying paprika peppers hanging against a whitewashed wall, every pod hyperreal: wrinkled lacquer-red skin, dusty shoulders, curled green stems, a split showing seeds. Around them, painted directly on the wall, a Kalocsa-style folk motif in vivid marker: cobalt, scarlet, leaf green and canary yellow, with dense satin-stitch-like hatching. The peppers cast soft real shadows over the decoration. Bright late morning light, cheerful saturation, a rich dialogue between handmade pattern and photographic produce.

A jade dagger hilt carved as a horse's head, rendered with the jewelled precision of a Mughal miniature. The pale celadon stone glows with translucent depth, its inlaid rubies and gold wire catching tiny pinpoint highlights. A one-hair brush builds every reflection in layered watercolour. Around it, a gold-flecked border with an inner band of lapis and a delicate scrolling margin frames the object like a manuscript page. The background is a flat saffron field. Intimate scale, courtly stillness, incredible patience in every mark.

An extreme close crop of a woman's face in profile: one eye, a single tear tracing mascara down a powdered cheek, a sliver of glossy cherry-red lip. Lit like a 1950s Technicolor melodrama, with saturated warm key light, a teal-tinted shadow side and a soft rose bloom. Dense, blended coloured pencil and watercolour capture every eyelash, pore, powder grain and the lensing of the tear. Background is a heavy velvet in deep peacock blue. Overwrought emotion, glamorous artifice, and microscopic realism of skin.

A massive rope-wrapped bow fender on an old tugboat fills the frame edge to edge, with no sky and no horizon. Its surface is built entirely from rolled-cord impressions: dense diagonal hatching in alternating directions, like twisted fibre pressed into wet clay, laid in graphite and dark iron-oxide pencil. The palette is earthen, raw sienna, burnt ochre and smoky umber, with flame-like soot blooms of charcoal licking up from the waterline where tar and diesel have stained it. Frayed strands and salt crust are picked out in pale bone. It should feel ancient and fired, a working object that reads like a vessel dug from a midden.

An old man's bald crown seen from behind, exactly eclipsing a bare tungsten bulb, so the scalp becomes a black disc of dense, velvety charcoal mass. Around it a corona of fine white hairs and drifting dust streams outward in long, curving pencil filaments, pearly titanium white thinning into pale chrome yellow and a faint coronal rose at the very limb. Each hair is a separate hairline stroke, wiry and slightly kinked, with tiny bright beads where they catch light. The surrounding room is a soft charcoal-grey gradient with no detail. The mood is solemn and astronomical, an ordinary head treated as a total eclipse.

A beige ball mouse and its coiled grey cord lying on a teal mousepad, rendered with hyperreal yellowed plastic, scuffed buttons and grime in the seams. Every edge follows 1990s operating-system bevel logic: a crisp white pen line on the top-left of each form and a charcoal-grey line on the bottom-right, filled with flat, even marker greys and desktop teal. A navy-to-azure title-bar strip runs across the top edge of the picture, with tiny square close buttons drawn as stiff little boxes. Shadows are hard and stepped rather than soft. The feeling is nostalgic, clerical and slightly absurd, pixel-precise but tactile.

A dented brass cezve and a small porcelain cup of Turkish coffee with a thick, bubbling crema, placed slightly low in the frame on a scratched walnut tray. Both are rendered hyperreal, with hammered brass reflections and grounds clinging to the rim. They sit within a gilded tezhip cartouche: delicate rumi and hatayi scrollwork in layered ochre and gold-yellow pen over a deep lapis watercolour ground, edged by hair-fine cinnabar and white contour rules. Ornament and object share the same jeweller-tight precision. The mood is courtly, meditative and fragrant.

A steep hillside of Valparaíso houses with corrugated walls, tangled power lines, a funicular and laundry on balconies, rendered with hyperreal perspective and weathering. Every surface reads as fabric appliqué stitched onto burlap: coarse crosshatched weave texture under flat watercolour patches of cobalt, mustard, coral and lime, each house outlined with dashed running-stitch pen marks in contrasting thread colours. A pale hessian sky shows its loose warp. Small figures climb the stairs. The feeling is communal, testimonial and stubbornly cheerful.

A low-angle view looking up at a wooden cargo bike parked under a pergola of photovoltaic tiles and climbing runner beans. The front crate overflows with dewless butterhead lettuces, radishes and a glass bottle of kombucha, every leaf vein and spoke rendered hyperreal. The medium is layered transparent watercolour in sap green, sunflower yellow, terracotta and copper-verdigris, tied together by clean, even ink contours in warm sepia. Dappled midday light falls through the panels in honeyed patches. The composition is busy but optimistic, with a hand-painted civic poster warmth and a sense of tended abundance rather than wilderness.

A tabby kitten asleep inside a torn shipping box, crammed against the corner of the frame. The cardboard is the star: kraft-brown marker fills, ragged ripped edges exposing the wavy inner flute drawn as precise rippling pencil lines, scuffed tape and a smudged barcode. The kitten's fur is built from short directional pencil strokes in warm grey and amber, so it echoes the cardboard's grain. Light is flat and diffuse, like a warehouse window. The palette stays narrow, with buff, tan, umber and a single pink nose. The mood is humble and tender, with packaging rendered as tenderly as the animal.
